proposals.relationship: Jacobson explicitly joins Roediger’s project of placing race at the center of the history of European immigration and assimilation.
proposals.evidence_note: Own Whiteness12 names Roediger jointly with KarenBrodkinSacks. Printed17–18 calls Wages of Whiteness important and subtle on political economy, class formation and psychology before identifying limits; actual285/n6–8 identifies the1991 Wages and separately credits other Roediger writing and joint work with JamesBarrett. This positive resource remains distinct from Jacobson’s criticism and does not establish complete agreement or sole influence. Original Roediger works unread.
primary_locators: Whiteness printed12 opening;17–18, paragraph beginning Roediger’s Wages;285 chapter1 notes6–8.

proposals.relationship: Jacobson argues that Roediger’s economic emphasis needs a longer chronology, finer distinctions among forms of whiteness and fuller attention to struggles outside class and labor.
proposals.evidence_note: Own17–19 praises Roediger and TheodoreAllen while spelling out three limits: distinctions among white/Caucasian/Celt, historical scale beyond selected decades, and elite or immigrant contests not fully explained by labor interests. Note13 at284 separately includes Roediger among sophisticated writers who sometimes treat Caucasian as unproblematic; that is a different terminological qualification, consolidated here without a duplicate same-pair critique. Jacobson does not reject class/economics or equate European immigrant oppression with AfricanAmerican exclusion (9). Allen retains separate credit; originals unread.
primary_locators: Whiteness printed17–19, especially18 three respects and19 Finally;285 chapter1 notes6–9;284 introduction note13;9 qualification.

proposals.relationship: Jacobson places Higham within an immigration historiography that, in his view, too readily translated earlier European racial distinctions into later ethnic categories.
proposals.evidence_note: Own introduction6–9 and actual note13 at284 explain a general historiographic problem and explicitly identify Higham’s Strangers alongside OscarHandlin and MaldwynAllenJones. Jacobson attributes this partly to the subfield’s formation during the consolidation of Caucasian identity, rather than simply ignoring the existence of racial prejudice. This is a bounded criticism of the framework and period categories, not a denial that Higham studied nativism or a refutation of his whole book. Note’s1865–1925 variant is not adopted as bibliography; original Higham book unread.
primary_locators: Whiteness printed6–9, especially8 first premise/n13;284 introduction note13 naming Higham’s Strangers.

proposals.relationship: Jacobson uses Du Bois’s definition of Blackness through Jim Crow to show how racial classification depends on social power and institutions.
proposals.evidence_note: Own printed110, following In Re Halladjian, explicitly turns to DuBois’s Dusk of Dawn and its dialogue on the race concept;301/n45 identifies the1960 Schocken edition of the1940 work,153. Printed124 also connects Schuyler’s account of racial allegiance to DuBois’s psychological-wage formulation, while18 discusses its use through Roediger. This is a specific conceptual resource and reception, not proof Jacobson adopts every DuBois or Roediger claim. Aptheker-edited Against Racism and Black Reconstruction receive distinct references; originals unread.
primary_locators: Whiteness printed110 parenthesis beginning DuBois captured this;301/n45;124 last paragraph;18/285 chapter1 n8.

proposals.relationship: Wolfe uses Jacobson’s formulation of republican inclusion and racial/gender exclusion as interdependent to develop his account of race and colonial power.
proposals.evidence_note: Own Wolfe2001,875/n29 quotes Jacobson22–23 while discussing Morgan’s slavery/freedom analysis; Morgan and DavidBrionDavis retain separate substantive credit. Wolfe adds a specific reservation about Jacobson’s treatment of liberalism, and893/n100 includes him among resources for the historical expansion of whiteness while preserving differences from anti-Black racialization. Positive use coexists with the separate qualification; original Jacobson22–23 not freshly read, so the quotation’s mediation through Wolfe is explicit.

proposals.relationship: Wolfe qualifies Jacobson’s account of republican inclusion and exclusion for leaving liberalism’s own credentials insufficiently interrogated.
proposals.evidence_note: Own875/n29 explicitly attaches this limited reservation to his otherwise substantive quotation of Whiteness22–23. This is a brief, scoped critical qualification, not an extended refutation of Jacobson’s book or a claim he ignored all relations of power. Wolfe’s positive use remains separately represented; his893/n100 distinction among racial regimes is not falsely treated as refuting Jacobson’s own9 warning against equating experiences. Original Jacobson22–23 remains unread here.
primary_locators: Wolfe2001 printed875 note29, parenthesis attached to MatthewFryeJacobson attribution;context874–876.

proposals.relationship: Gerstle draws on Jacobson’s account of racialized nationality to situate racial exclusion within the early American republic.
proposals.evidence_note: Own Gerstle1999 opening1280 explicitly names MatthewJacobson and RogersSmith for constructions of American nationality present in the Constitution and1790 naturalization rule;note1 identifies Whiteness1998 alongside Smith,Rogin,Roediger,Takaki,Horsman and Higham’s separate resources. This is a specified historiographical use, not sole influence or endorsement of every part of Whiteness. The original book’s22–23 section remains unread here; dated legal interpretations are attributed to the article.
primary_locators: Gerstle1999 printed1280 opening paragraph and note1;1281 continuation.

proposals.relationship: In Tunc’s comparative account, Jacobson and Bederman extend the study of whiteness into cultural and political histories of racial representation, masculinity and civilization.
proposals.evidence_note: Explicit named scholarly mediation limited to Tunc’s substantive author abstract, which compares Whiteness of a Different Color and Manliness and Civilization, linking archival sources with literary criticism, material culture and gender theory. This is an editorial teaching comparison supported at abstract level, not mutual influence, a shared school or an exclusive origin claim. Full2008 review and complete originals unread in this dossier.
primary_locators: Tunc2008 institutional author abstract, paragraph beginning Prior to the mid-1990s, and named book discussion.
